blocks.x: I was a banjo and guitar too, but that boy could play some banjo.
Who was that?
That Harris Desdune was banned, was that?
Oh yeah, Harris Banjo played banjo. He could play some banjo.
Well, how old would you be, Hal, when you first picked up your... I'm not taking lessons around nine, ten years old. With the T.O.?
No, with Professor Nickerson.
On Friday?
Yeah, I started with Professor Nickerson.
Is that the same piano teacher that Professor Minetta tells about?

Well, Professor Nickerson was a great violin player. Very wonderful violin player, but he taught all instruments. His daughter, Camille Nickerson, was a very fine pianist. She's in Howard University now, in Washington, I think. Well, I'd like to meet her. I'd like to meet her. She should remember, because she used to make me sing all them old Creole songs. When I was small, I knew all them songs. My mother used to learn them to me, you know, Creole songs. And I used to say she'd play them on the piano.
Now, he'd be an old gentleman at that time.
Oh, yeah, he was an old man. He had his goatees and his mustache, and they was white then. Torn and white, anyway, yeah.
Well, how long did you go to him for about that?
Oh, I went to him, I guess, about a year. Until he didn't like playing no outside music. So I would play what he taught.
I have so many movies on the Boeber Street and behind the melody. You have a picture of Moonlight Serenade. Yeah, I have a little bit of things. He's tall as you and that.
You were saying that when Brother played the blues, first one or two came around and then... Everybody started. And they were just watching him...

That was the place, the first place I took a drink in my life. They were just watching him play. That's right. They enjoyed it so much. They enjoyed him and he was playing. I mean, he could... In other words, he could stop a dance when he got ready. Yeah. Yeah. And he left us and we picked up a woman by the name of Vivian from Atkins, Kansas. And she was very good paying up there too. She came up with a band that we came down there. And you know, until the band... Things like a little tough and bad. But she was a very good paying up there too. Someday I'd like you to get this band to play up from... Best listeners of Harry Faggner to it. Yeah, yeah. First player with Desdun and us. He could sing and play. Didn't have no mic, you know. If they weren't in a megaphone. Yeah. I mean, you can hear them all over the place. A little bit of things. And his cousin was playing with us at that time. Two out of... Let me see. I think he was playing in Lucian Johnson's place. I'm trying to... No. He was playing before Lucian Johnson. Very good clarinet. He played clarinet, piano and saxophone. His name is Warren. He's the one of that. And bass on that's where Patrick stands. Very, very good. And if you ever want to know something about Catherine, I'll tell you who's played Maddie Reyes, banjo. I can take it back by the skin field. Yeah. That's a good thing. Mm-hmm. But in them days, George Ganova was in there with him too, you know. Yeah, George was good. George always could play a band. He can still play a part of his son, yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Mm-hmm.

Yeah, I went to Tony's house last night, Tony Sanders here, to his barber shop. He's still cutting hair. Tried to find it when I was playing with him on the Pelican, you know. I played several jobs with him on the Pelican. All I remember, Ellie Begarden was playing drum with him.
You said, what was the Pelican? You mean that?
That was on the corner of the...
Oh, you mean that place up on Rampart, yeah.
Yeah, on the corner of Rampart and Grab, yeah.
It sounded like you said on the Pelican like it was a boat or something.

Well, it was on the Pelican. Was it a roof? No, it was not a roof. It was just a dance office where we'd go. We said, we're going on the Pelican tonight, you know. Yeah. And the next block was Astoria. Yeah, I remember that.
Yeah.

Well, at the Pelican, when I had the Pelican, when I had the Pelican, the Pelican annex on the bottom, you see. And when the fellas come in at night off the boat and bands come in town, well, that's where they used to go jam all night long.
I won't say dinner there. They must not have had segregation those days. What? That's when Bunk Johnson first came to town. Well, I tell you now, a long time ago,

things were mighty nice around town. That was 1942. I always did go hours ago. I mean, because I know how to care of myself and take care of myself. But I mean, people didn't go all foolish like that. People are foolish, you know. We used to have some boys across the street at my house. The boys would start playing saxophone. My brother and I was playing music and live across the street at my house. We used to go to school together every morning. We used to stand, just carve a school around on the Man Street. Well, it was Willa McG Rogers, I think. And we used to stand in front of the school and wait until we come and buy them to school and even walk home together. Yeah, they never had a lot of, I mean, it's just, it's something, I don't know, something went haywire. When did you first go on the boat, sir?
How did that come about?

Well, a friend of mine, we went to school together, but the name was Luis Andre. Well, my brother was playing, stopped playing the violin. He was still playing the violin, but he was taking trumpet lessons, and I was taking cladid lessons, and Luis wanted to play saxophone. In other words, he was on the first one I ever played a piece on. The first piece I ever played on a saxophone, believe it or not, it was a two-land swing. It was a very first piece on, pre- and St. Philip, next to Peter Claiborne's Church. It was St. Anne's Church then. And he went on a boat with Sun White and Em, I think I was at the college end, and wanted me to go, so when he came back, he told me he didn't like the job. You know, he had just started. So when I went, I stayed on that, telling him, man, man, I think that's about three or four months, remember me?
What year was it about now?

That must have been around maybe 23, 24, maybe 21, I don't know. I was a youngster, I know, because I tell you, we didn't have nothing to do in the day at all. Sun White was washing dishes in the kitchen, and playing with the band at night. And I would be so tired, I was a youngster, just out of, you know, going to school. I was a little active. I used to go and help the rouserbots carry the stave.
And you were boxing too?

No, I used to box at school in the middle of it. When I, Captain used to enjoy seeing me, you know, getting nine with them rouserbots, you know, and carry the stave. I mean, he gave me a, told everybody on the boat, anything you want to give him, any concession stand, he said, you don't pay for nothing on this boat. He said, that's a terrible youngster. And then we'd play at night, we'd play excursions from Columbia, Columbia, Mississippi, you know, and, I mean, Louisiana, and up around Arkansas. And we'd get to Cameron, Arkansas, we'd play that excursion, and then we'd turn around and come back. Well, they'd pick up freight and drop freight off on the way, you see. And at night, sometimes I'd take my clarinet and go down with them, down there by them rouserbots, because I always was a good mixer, you know, everybody was a human being, a human being to me. I would play a little blues for them, and they'd get paid off in Baton Rouge. Everybody would get paid off in Baton Rouge, you know, just give me a thousand, just give me two, baby, you know.
Just by yourself on clarinet, or?

Yeah, just by myself, just by myself. You can clarinet then? Yeah. Mm-hmm. I wasn't that great, but I mean, I could play that melody. You still need the blues. I could play that melody. Making that money, I could play that melody, you see. So I tell you, that's why Deren's Boy, and Lewis Gallo, and Bill Phillips, that's why they hired me at the Japanese Tea Garden at Melon Boy, because I could read them what I see. And they'd buy that music, and I'd read it for them, you see.
What was that Japanese tea garden like? Was it over the water, out in the camp?

Well, it was right by the water. The Japanese tea garden set right, no, right at the, right by the lake, you see. And then, well, you had to go on the run, or the walkway to get to the camp. It was not on the camp, it was, you know, right on land, but right at the foot of the lake.
Where the railroad went out through, the Spokin Mary?
Yeah, Spokin Mary went on.
Right close to the Japanese?

Close to the camp, close to it. On the side of the baudouin? Yeah, no, Spokin Mary didn't come all the way in front of the Japanese Tea Garden. They had a little, it comes about where Moreau's Grocery is right now. Yeah, I know. And the grocery's there right now. Me and Sidney Miner, you and my brother, and the band, Joe Cliff, I never, Reuben McClendon, McClendon, that he's away from the Southern Moccan Company right now. Well, we were playing at Moreau's Camp in 1928, at Lilwood's. And Moreau's got the same grocery there now. He's still at the same grocery there. Yeah. I wonder if it is still there. I don't know if the grocery's there, but I think the family's still there. We'll take a ride at that, see, sometime, you know. Yeah, I think it may still be there. You know what we said last night? Well, if the place is torn down, it's torn down recently, because I passed there, I guess, six or eight months ago, I would say, or maybe longer. And I look at that place, I say, oh, Moreau, you know, to myself, like that. They just have a very, a pretty good saxophone player. There's a player next door at a place called Baradice, next to the Japanese T-Guard. Boy, I've heard of that. His name was Hickman. And sometime I say, I say, sometime I'm going to play like that, man. But I don't know what happened. Eleven o'clock every night, they was closing up. We'd be there at three or four o'clock in the morning, and then Bob Wachers would say sometime, look, y'all want to play a little breakfast dance or picnic or something? He'd say, yeah. I'd call, get on the phone and call my mother and tell her, we have to play a breakfast dance or something, and he'd come in town and get some of his friends to come on back out there and we'd be playing until 10, 11, 12 o'clock in the day. So I don't know what happened. That's why I always believe a man should play a little melody. Some, let people know they're playing. That's what's the cause of that. That place we throw some nice 11, 12 o'clock. Everybody, probably next door could hear what I was playing on the saxophone. But not taking nothing away from him, it was pretty good.

As you were saying, it's good to catch up on a few of these little things that we might forget later. Who was the fellow that you told us about that took the clarinet apart and ended up playing on the mouthpiece?
Paul Moyer. Paul was a drummer, huh? He was a fellow that played with Paul Moyer. No, played with an old man Moyer. That's his son I'm talking about. Paul was a drummer.
What was his son's name? He wanted to play the clarinet.

I used to go play with him and they had a trumpet player by the name of La Quasi very often. Oh, was Paul Moyer's son that took the- Old man Paul Moyer. Not this Paul Moyer that died sometime ago. That's the one who used to take the clarinet apart and play all apart. That's the one that took it apart.
That's right.

He used to lay on the floor lay on the bench and take one piece at a time and put it down and take the other piece and put it down and take the other piece and just go and play until he get to the mouthpiece. He was just enjoying that. Oh, he just enjoyed that. Yeah, I learned a lot of foolishness from him. Yeah. And Paul was playing drum then. He was a little bit of kid playing drum with his dad in the band.
Well, wait a minute.

If he was playing drum. I said Paul Moyer played drum, but Oynice Moyer was the clarinet. Oynice. Oynice, Paul Moyer's brother. Yeah, because when I first went to the opera house, that's who I went to the opera house with, you know. With Paul Moyer playing drum and Sammy Hopkins playing piano.
Which opera house? Where's that?
On the corner of Toulouse and Boevin. Oh, French Opera House ball.
Oh, yeah.

I was sitting on my step. I told my wife, I said, after I come out to Navy, you know, well, sticking to that music so hard, I mean, blowing so much. I was playing baritone with one of the concerted bands. I was playing baritone and clarinet with the big orchestra. I was playing tenor with the parade band. And I was playing tenor with one of the concerted bands. And I was playing alto in my Dixieland band. See, I had a Dixieland band. And the chief, sometime we had to play a crew dance. And the dance with officers Sam Knight, where the chief would take the band, the big band, I'd take the Dixieland band and go play for the crew.
Now, this was the Opera House bar, but one is still there.
It's still there. Yeah. I played there about three years, every night.

When you talk about Opera House, well, you're going to say something about a theater. You mean the old French Opera House? Yeah, but other people, I wanted to ask, this is interrupting and changing the subject again, that theater over here on Rampart Street. I forgot the name of that thing. You mean what Schumann had when I was playing Piran?
That's before you. Yeah, I played at the Silver Slipper, you mean that's, Yeah, I guess that's. Because Piran was directing my band at the Silver Slipper.
Where was the Silver Slipper then? Was there on the Rampart?

Right there, right, no, the Silver Slipper's on Boyleburn. The Bourbon, the one, yeah. See, right where, what's the name of that, where, where, where, where, the Dixieland band. That's the Dream Room. Dream Room, that's right, that was the Silver Slipper. Well, what about this theater? I might have one of those Silver Slippers home, no, they used to give us silver in there. I didn't know I had it for many years.
What was this theater on Rampart Street? Somebody else told me once, but we don't have anything about it in there.
I forgot the name of it, yeah.
I mean, where was it, do you remember?
The theater, what, what, what, what Schumann Hall, you mean? What, the matter is, I was playing by the Silver Slipper?

Yeah, I mean, what was that little theater? Was it a, was it ever a dance hall first or something? Well, I don't, no, I don't think so. Seems like somebody told me that once was a little French theater, and then it later became a dance hall, or maybe it had been a dance hall and they turned it into a theater. Well, I, that's beyond me, no.
You don't remember anything about that.
That's beyond me, no. Something like that, no, that went on, I forget what it is. No, I don't remember that. We'll find somebody on, tell us someday.

Getting back to that, when I first went to the opera house, I went with, it was Paul Moyer, and the Sam Hopkins playing piano. I told him I wasn't gonna rest him for a couple of weeks, but right with the Silver Slipper, was just making so much money, just making, oh, I guess, $40, $50, $90, $90, $10. Oh, yeah, yeah, yeah. And when I went to the opera house, the scale was $6. And when I stayed there, and first night I went there, a man asked me, he said, can you read? I said, read a little. He said, I got this number, no, it was in Washington Square. He said, several bands there, he said. I don't seem to get nobody wanted to play. I said, well, if you don't, you don't own a place and want the number playing, I'll play it. So he'd give it to me, he said, you think you'll have it ready for next week's rehearsal? When I look at the thing, Rose of Washington Square, he said, anybody could play it. I guess the one who was there just didn't want to play it, see? I know good what a captain played if he wanted to play it, you know? So I said, your wife got a costume made? He said, yeah. I said, well, she can do it tonight if she wants. What do you mean? I said, that's what I said. So I went on and played Don once, and he said, well, I'll be doggone. And he'd come to me and say, your son was raised a dollar tonight. I thought nine, he said, yeah. Yeah. Yeah. So, well, I played there for him, and then when he sold the place, the Baron King, I stayed there with him. I played for Stormy. And then when she left, Dolly Faye came and played there for them. And then Nick Connell took the place. I played a while for him, then, but they had different ideas. They were my chief man, you know? So, and then that. Did anybody ever tell you about the trumpet player around him by the name of Kimball?
Yeah, I've heard, I don't know much about him, but I've heard the name. He's heard the trumpet player.

He's heard the name, yeah. Oh, when he left here, he went to Shreveport. We had to start the end in Shreveport. That's where I met him. I met him around here once or twice, but last I seen him, that's where he was at, and he's not where he was dead.
Yeah, I've heard of him, but never did, got to hear him or know him.
He's very good trumpet player.
Yeah, I've heard of him very good. What type of player was he? Was he a good musician or mostly a headman?
Good musician and headman, just like Mani Parade. Good musician and headman.
You might tell us a little bit about the Claiborne Williams band. You were telling us outside that you were in the Navy with George Williams. With George Williams.

Very, very first class musician. And he's back in, up in Baton Rouge. He's teaching, yeah. My wife teaches school. I think he's teaching music at some school, I think. I'm not sure, but I don't know. He's also selling instruments and everything. Yeah. We played, he was standing on the corner of Jackson Avenue. The last time we played that big parade, we left him, Drys and Phillip. We had four or five bands out.
Yeah?

Sure. But he was standing on Jackson Avenue and, what is it, Parade? Block of Four, LaSalle. He was standing right on that corner, because I walked out the parade and went and spoke. He said, I got to leave right away, otherwise I'd follow you to talk with you, you know, because you wouldn't come to Baton Rouge and play with him. He was a very good musician. Is that this year? Oh, no, that was last year. Well, there was, there was, uh, King John.
I remember one last year that way it started. It was a Mason's parade. Yeah, right.
Prince Hall, I guess. No, it was not Prince Hall. I think it was King George. Oh, yeah, the one that had. No, St. John. St. On Phillip and Dry.
Yeah, I know, where they had the pub houses.

Yeah, but last time we left there with that big parade, he was standing on Jackson Avenue. Russ was in the Navy, Russ. Russ, Henry Russ, Said. Oh, yeah. We had a very good trombone player and music teacher from Wallace Collins and Boatron Adams.
How long were you in the Navy there, Henry?
Well, I was in there for three years and three months. Three years and three months. Right across there. We stayed in boot camp for 16 weeks, but we can't have the rest of the time.
Oh, you were at the Cross River there.
My brother was with the band at the Lakefront with Daryl Poinnell, Willie Humphrey and them people. Yeah.
And then you played in the Navy band? Yeah. Navy band. Yeah.

Well, after the Navy, they was not making a reserve Navy band. I got in the inactive reserve and when the Army was making a band at Spencer, a very good bass player, teaching music in New Iberraighton, I think. Well, he told me, he said, I'm gonna get an Army band here in the band again. He said, with your rating, he said, you'll be way up there. So I said, I think I will. So I got in the Navy, an Army band then, and Army, Melvin C. Bryant, a music teacher at Dillard University, had a charge in the band. Well, I was assistant, I was a master of the Navy band and also an Army band. Had a wonderful time, plenty of good music to read and play, you know. Had some good musicians in that band. Yeah. This boy was playing bassoon with us, teaching music at St. Augustine now on London Avenue. Oh, wow. Yeah. Yeah, very good. Hampton. Oh, yeah. And this boy, very good clarinet player, is teaching at 35 school right now, Harold Batiste. Oh, yeah. Yeah, he was an Army band, a very fine band. Morett was playing trumpet. This little kid that lived on that street was playing with Tommy Ridgerton now. He was playing with a very good band. Very bad. But I don't think none of them was compared to Navy band, man. I mean, a band as a whole. Yeah. I mean, man for man was different, but a band as a whole, no. Well, we had more time to, all right, we had more time to rehearse us. We commissioned ships all through the day. Sometimes we fish and leave that 4.30 and 25 minutes after, for the phone ring. One of the officers, the captain or somebody wants some music for that night. That ain't that. Yeah, that ain't that. Well, it started us off rough. Well, we first hit here, two days before, the day before Christmas Eve. They told us when y'all, when we hit y'all, y'all gone. Whenever they take our 9, they leave, you see. Waiting to get back home. So, the chief told us, he said, well, tomorrow we gotta play a Christmas Eve party. All the people on the base bring in their family, their children and everything, got Christmas free out there. He said, chief, but the band are leaving together here. So, we had to get together to go play that Christmas Eve party. Everybody was, ooh, we gonna have a wonderful band here on this base. I said, Lord, I didn't know what to say, you know, but they enjoyed it. So, well, time went by, everything went on fine. Everything went fine.
Well, you mentioned outside some, who was it that Saeed's brother-in-law or something? Oh, Benny Benoit.

I was playing with him with the Liberty Band, but I gnawly passed. That's years ago. I remember when I gnawly passed and myself, we were playing at the Crystal Palace in Depression time up on Clio and Radha, near Drys. And all the boys from Browns, the ice cream company used to come there, you know. And I know I told him, son, you don't drink now. I said, no, son. He said, well, don't turn no beer on. When they bring you the beer, give it to me. When the boys bring the ice cream, I give it to you. So, I ate the ice cream, he drank the beer. Yeah. But he was a very fine drummer. He reminds, he and L.E.P. guys remind me, I close my eyes, I sound like the same people playing drums. You know, when they got that good, bright leg and they put that time down, let's stay at that.
And it sounds like, who did you say?
He and L.E.P. guys are players alike. Oh, alike.
Oh, I thought you were going to say they sound like somebody else. No, he and L.E.P.
Yeah, they do. Yeah, that's right.
They're alike.

They're alike. They had some nice times in the band. They had, Zeddy Johnson was playing saxophone with them too. And a fellow by the name of Tom Copeland lived down around Maurice Durand House. He was playing bass. And Albert Francis' wife was playing piano. Albert Francis drummer, his wife was playing piano in his band. And this fellow played trumpet, what they call Cuckoo. I think his right name is Tavern. Yeah. I got a picture of him home. And he was playing trumpet. Used to get plenty of weight. Plenty of weight. But he used to come at my house and get them and my mom used to tell him, you can take them if you're going to bring them back home. You had to bring them back home. Yeah. Well, mine used to have to come get me and bring me back home too. Minor would play bass. Oh yeah. Come get me and my little brother and have to bring us back home if you can take us.
Yeah.
Also, this drummer lived back on Gravity Street with that Peter Williams. Yeah. Yeah.
He had to bring me back home too.

Yeah. Yeah. He had to bring me back home too. Yeah. Yeah. Also, this drummer lived back on Gravity Street with that Peter Williams. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. He had to bring me back home too. Mm-hmm. You know.
Another thing you were telling us was that Earl Bostic, you say, got a lot of his stuff from you now.

Well, Earl Bostic was very fast on the saxophone. Very fast. Very good musician and everything. But the style he played on the record, that's the style that Thereto Poino used to play around here. Yeah. That's the style. Every time I heard Earl Bostic's record, I said that. That's right. Have you seen Pernell lately or? I saw him at the banquet we had. Oh, yeah.
Somebody else thought maybe told me that he's recovering a little bit now.

Well, I don't know. He and I had a personal friend of mine. We'd come up together, very personal friend of mine. I'd sit in his car and talk to him at least 45 minutes after we left the banquet. And he's talking to the doctor, so he'd play 15 minutes a day. He plays clarinet, very good clarinet player. And he bought his saxophone at night and he played about 15 minutes, that was it. But he still got something. He still played.
How's his memory? Is his memory all right?

Pretty good, because you could tell by the head numbers he played, because when he picked up his horn, I would stand right there by him, because I always used to tell him, like him or St. George, I said, I see him at the horn, let me play. You know? I mean, kid wasn't that like that. He might tell me why I'm playing. He said, give me this horn. But I went stand by him, and listened at him, and he was just playing a couple of head numbers, and he was right in there.
Right in there. And people sang it, sometimes he'd just say, couldn't remember how a certain little simple tune went.

Well, he say, you say that did him good, that Sunday. He said, I didn't think I could play in time even. He said, how did? I said, you sound like you're never just stop playing for us, I'm concerned. It really was good. Yeah, sure, very good. We ought to go down to his house one time.
We want to interview him, but I was wondering about, also, you know, we don't like to bother somebody if they're not feeling it.
We go down and talk, and we ask him how long he could sit down and talk, and then when he say how long he could talk, well, then he'd blow.
Even if it's only 15 minutes a day.
Yeah, yeah.
Get him on tape.
The doctor told me he could blow 15 minutes a day.
He could talk in 15 minutes all right, too.

Yeah, right. See, he was playing with Sid and Desiree in a long time, he and my brother like Tom Johnson. But Tom's in California, too, a very good saxophone player. We had a saxophone, a clarinet player, was a very, very good, well, actually, if you've ever heard of it, by the name of Felix Goff. He used to play with Rizzly, when we were playing with Rizzly, old man Porter was playing who the former was, with Rizzly. And this boy named Felix Goff, he could play. Man, he could play some time. I thought, you know, sometime you might have run across him or his name. Is he still around? I don't know, I never heard of him for many years. He used to like to travel to circuses and shows, you know, like that rough, real rough life. He was rough, too, but he could play. Yeah. Another boy we got out of Jackson, Mississippi, Sam Tom, we picked up Brennan Montgomery. A boy called Eugene Porter. You ever hear of that?
Sam, you know, we talked to brother, you see.

What did he play? We played, we played, we played, we played, we played, we played, we played, we played tenor saxophone. And, we had to coach him to get up to take a course after he got the fright off him. He was tough, I'm telling you. And then he had McLaren, no time, no time, no time, I said a couple of months. He was sitting in the back of that plan and taking slow moves and things. Yeah, a couple of months. We had him at a bar on Brookhaven College, E.W. Brown. His daddy was over the Rabbitfoot Show one time. And Brookhaven, Brookhaven, a few miles from there, right in that neighborhood. But, yeah, he could play some time there. Very good.
You said you played with Georgia Boyle.

Yeah, well, at the Willing, Georgia Boyle, you were there at the Willing. And, he said, now I'm going to take the Clarenor and the Luce when he fell out. And talk to you, like you holding a conversation there, and you want to take the Clarenor and the Luce, you know? And you can have a Spanish. Yeah, he was alright. He always had a terrible cough though. But he didn't. He could play it. Did he smoke? He was smoking. Oh, I know. He was smoking. Drink like that. Yeah. He had TB or anything, didn't he? Yeah, he died. The person had consumption TB or something.
Somebody told us about the other day.
He always had a heavy cough. But, Brother Coleman, he used to live two blocks of me. We were little kids on Arlene Street. He had a privilege to play piano there.
Brother Coleman, imagine. He was Thomas Bell, yeah.

Yeah, but he played a lot of jobs with him. He played a lot of jobs with him. He played a lot of jobs with him. Did he smoke? Did he smoke? Did he smoke? Did he smoke? Did he smoke? Oh, I know. He was full of smoking, drinking, yeah. I know. We were little kids on Arlene Street. He had a privilege to play piano there. Brother Coleman, imagine. He was Thomas Bell. Yeah.
But he played a lot of jobs with him. He does clarinet after he died.
Yeah, really. Yeah. We never gave a clarinet.
Yeah.
Well, I wasn't wondering if he had TB.
Well, it could be sterile. You never know that everything would be clean.
Yeah. That would be great. No way.
Speaking about clarinets, I wonder if you ever knew what these swells use

Well, I tell you, now I couldn't tell you which string he used, but he always told me, very seldom you catch two people using the sand and shredder reeds, they're like in the sandbag, and he said, very seldom, because sometimes he'd buy me a, I'd give him a little number two, and you'd have to make it, three, four, I'd get a number three, and you'd have to cut it down or something like that, you know, tell me a line, I'd just try to read, you know, some people, you know, just go by and shredder, you gotta by reading, you know, bring it down to ready warm, you know. Do you still do that, do you remember? You know, sometimes, I used to use a three and a half reed, and I don't know why, but sometimes I can use a three and a half, but most of the time I use a three, and sometimes I catch a tree running around the nose, most of the time, you know, late I catch some trees, but always use a violabrator reading, and always, to me, a violabrator, and all and every reed line, and the red line, and the dure and everything, but always can't be a flint, vibrate.
And did you use the same flint, you ever mean, you ever find that, you ever go?
Yeah, but a nut slant flint, you ever find it?
Well, what flint was you used to have a flint in it?
I used it about two and a half.
Oh, you were chopped to me.

Two and a half, but when I was playing a lot of numbers, like sometimes I would be playing simply numbers or something like that, you know, I was playing a soul kind of plug, I would try to work a three, another three out, you know, because it was easy to make the high notes. The soft reed, you gotta use your lip more, you know, tighten up and loosen your lip. The stiff reed, you know, you can play it more as well. I don't mean the two-step, I mean the one just about it. Yeah, I know.
I wondered if you ever knew what you were before, you ever have your notes?

No, no, no, no. I really, I really, I really, I really, I really, I really, I really, I really, I really, I really, I really, I really, I really, I really, I really, I really, I really, I really, I really, I really, I really, I really, I really, I really, I really, I really, I really, Thank you.

See the boy or something, at the wheelhead, the proprietor, the place. When Willie Dunnberg hit that door and they do that, shoot it off. And give him five hours and give him another the next day. So what Willie did, Willie just bought him a few cheap hats, you know? And when the man shoot it off, he'll give him five hours the next night. He put on one of them with a cheap one in his head.

segments.title: Harris Desdunes and his banjo playing
segments.summary: Dejan recalls Harris Desdunes as a fine banjo player.

segments.title: Lessons with Professor Nickerson and his daughter Camille
segments.summary: Dejan started lessons around age nine or ten with Professor Nickerson, a violinist who taught all instruments; he recalls Camille Nickerson and Creole songs, and quit after about a year over outside music.

segments.title: Brother's blues, Vivian, and a band's players
segments.summary: Garbled recollection of a player who could stop a dance with the blues, a woman player named Vivian, a clarinet-playing cousin Warren and other bandmates; he also mentions seeing Tony Sanders and playing with him.

segments.title: The Pelican dance hall on Rampart and Gravier
segments.summary: Dejan explains that 'the Pelican' was a dance place on Rampart, with an annex where visiting bandsmen jammed all night; he also recalls schoolmates and boyhood.

segments.title: Going on the riverboat with Sun White and playing for the roustabouts
segments.summary: Through friend Luis Andre he joined a riverboat band, washing dishes and playing excursions; he played blues on clarinet for roustabouts, and was hired at the Japanese Tea Garden because he could read.

segments.chapter: Dance jobs and the opera house
segments.title: The Japanese Tea Garden at Milneburg and Moreau's camp
segments.summary: He describes the tea garden's lakeside location, the Smoky Mary train, and playing at Moreau's camp in 1928 with Sidney Miner, his brother and others, often playing late and into breakfast dances.

segments.chapter: Dance jobs and the opera house
segments.title: Paul Moyer and the clarinet player who took his horn apart
segments.summary: Dejan sorts out the Moyers: old man Moyer's son took his clarinet apart piece by piece while playing; Paul played drums and Oynice was the clarinetist.

segments.chapter: Dance jobs and the opera house
segments.title: The French Opera House and Navy band instruments
segments.summary: Dejan first went to the French Opera House with Paul Moyer and Sammy Hopkins; he also lists the many horns he played in Navy bands, and says he played at the opera house bar three years.

segments.chapter: Dance jobs and the opera house
segments.title: The Silver Slipper and the forgotten theater on Rampart
segments.summary: Piron directed Dejan's band at the Silver Slipper (the Dream Room on Bourbon); the interviewer asks about a small theater on Rampart, which Dejan cannot recall.

segments.chapter: Dance jobs and the opera house
segments.title: Pay and bosses at the opera house after the Silver Slipper
segments.summary: He compares Silver Slipper pay with the $6 scale at the opera house, recounts proving he could read, and lists the owners he played for.

segments.chapter: Dance jobs and the opera house
segments.title: Trumpeter Kimball
segments.summary: Dejan describes Kimball, a good trumpeter and headman, who went to Shreveport.

segments.title: Claiborne Williams band and George Williams, a Navy bandmate
segments.summary: He praises George Williams, a first-class musician now teaching in Baton Rouge whom he saw at a parade, and mentions other Navy colleagues.

segments.title: Three years in the Navy band and the Army band afterward
segments.summary: Dejan served three years and three months in the Navy, then joined an Army band at Camp Plauche; he compares it unfavorably to the Navy band, and tells of the first Christmas Eve party.

segments.title: Benny Benoit, the Crystal Palace and a band's members
segments.summary: He recalls playing with the drummer Benoit at the Crystal Palace in Depression time, compares drummers, and lists the members of a band and the boys who came to fetch him.

segments.title: Earl Bostic's style and a ailing friend's 15 minutes a day
segments.summary: Dejan says Bostic's recorded style was that of Theodore Purnell, a close friend now recovering who can play 15 minutes a day; the interviewers consider recording him.

segments.title: Felix Goff, Eugene Porter and other saxophonists in his band
segments.summary: He names clarinet and sax players from his Desvigne and Ridgley days, including Felix Goff and tenor man Eugene Porter from Jackson, Mississippi.

segments.title: Georgia Boy, Brother Coleman and illness among clarinetists
segments.summary: Discussion of a clarinetist with a heavy cough who died of consumption, and of Brother Coleman, a pianist from his childhood street.

segments.title: Reeds, mouthpieces and strengths he used
segments.summary: Dejan talks about the reeds he used, mainly a three, sometimes a three and a half or two and a half, and how soft versus stiff reeds affect the lip.

segments.title: Willie's cheap hats story
segments.summary: Fragmentary anecdote about a man shooting off hats and Willie buying cheap ones.
